index.title: Introduction
index.desc: gpui-query is async state management for GPUI, the Rust framework behind Zed. Declarative queries with caching, retries, and cancellation built in.

blocks.html: gpui-query is an async state management library for GPUI, the framework behind the Zed editor.

gpui-query brings the async state management patterns of TanStack Query to GPUI. It provides a declarative way to fetch, cache, synchronize, and update server state without manual lifecycle management.

items.html: Zero boilerplate: Define a query, bind it to a view.
Automatic caching: Responses are cached and deduplicated.
Built-in retry and error handling: Failed requests are retried with configurable policies.
Observer pattern: Reactively update your UI when data changes.
Designed for GPUI: Direct integration with GPUI’s entity and view system.
Install gpui-query in your project.
Follow the Quick Start guide to make your first query.
Explore the API Reference for detailed documentation.
Read the Guides for patterns and best practices.

getting-started/installation.title: Installation
getting-started/installation.desc: Install gpui-query in a Rust GPUI app: add the crate, register the global QueryClient, and verify your setup with a first query.

blocks.html: gpui-query is a Cargo crate. This page covers adding it to a GPUI project, choosing the right feature flags, and installing a QueryClient as a GPUI Global so the hooks can share a single cache.
Run cargo add in your crate:

blocks.code: cargo add gpui-query

blocks.html: or add it by hand to Cargo.toml:

blocks.code:
[dependencies]
gpui-query = "0.3.1"

blocks.html: gpui-query depends on gpui as a workspace dependency. It does not ship gpui itself. Your app already brings gpui in, and gpui-query links against the same version.
The crate is split into four layers, each behind a feature flag:

blocks.html: client is on by default, so cargo add gpui-query is enough to get the registry. To use the ergonomic hooks from your components, enable the hook feature:

blocks.code:
[dependencies]
gpui-query = { version = "0.3.1", features = ["hook"] }
cargo add gpui-query --features hook

blocks.html: Enable hook unless you drive the QueryClient manually. Reach for core alone when you need the state machine without a GPUI dependency (a library, a CLI that reasons about cached state, or unit tests). Add persist when you want to save and restore the cache across restarts (gpui-query = { features = ["hook", "persist"] }).
Two standalone crates extend gpui-query without adding dependencies to the core:

items.html: gpui-query-persist is a reference disk adapter. FilePersister atomically writes a PersistSnapshot to disk (JSON or bincode) with a tolerant load. cargo add gpui-query-persist. See Persistence: reference adapter.
gpui-query-http turns a server’s Cache-Control header into a CachePolicy (“server wins”) and layers an in-memory HttpCache over any HTTP backend. cargo add gpui-query-http. See HTTP cache headers.

blocks.html: gpui-query-http depends on gpui-query core-only (no GPUI). gpui-query-persist enables the full persist + client + hook stack. Both publish independently.

QueryClient is a GPUI Global. Install it once during app setup. From then on, the query hooks (use_query and use_infinite_query) route resource creation through it for shared caching, deduplication, and garbage collection. use_mutation creates a standalone entity and only registers it with the global, so GC still tracks it and use_mutation_state can find it.
QueryClient::new() uses the default policies (Ttl { ttl_ms: 60_000 }, LatestWins). Override them with with_policies and tune the garbage-collection window with with_gc_time:

If a query hook (use_query and its variants) runs before a QueryClient is installed, it panics in debug builds. In release builds it falls back to a standalone entity, with no shared cache, deduplication, or GC. (use_mutation and use_infinite_query fall back to a standalone entity without panicking.) Always install the client during app startup.
From any context, read the client back to confirm the global is set:
That is the entire setup: add the crate, enable hook, install a QueryClient global. With that in place, the Quick Start shows your first end-to-end query.

getting-started/quick-start.title: Quick Start
getting-started/quick-start.desc: Write your first gpui-query query and mutation in a GPUI app: fetch data with use_query, render each status, and dispatch a write with use_mutation.

blocks.html: This page walks through a minimal end-to-end query: define a fetcher, subscribe to it with use_query, read the status and data, and render. Then a tiny use_mutation example so you can see the full loop.
It assumes you have already installed gpui-query and set up a QueryClient global.
gpui-query is built around three pieces:

items.html: A fetcher: an async function that knows how to load some data. gpui-query owns everything else: caching, deduplication, retries.
use_query: a hook you call from a view’s constructor (not in render). It fetches the first time, subscribes the view to the result, and returns an Entity you read during render.
The QueryClient: a global registry that shares results across views, so concurrent requests for the same key collapse into one fetch (invalidation, TTL expiry, and forced refetches fetch it again).

blocks.html: Data is cached under a QueryKey. Two views asking for the same key read from the same cached entity.
Both the data type T and the error type E must be Clone + Send + Sync + 'static, and E must be Debug. A cheap stand-in for the error is the crate’s QueryError, but you can use your own.

A fetcher is a Fn(QuerySignal) -> Future<Output = Result<T, E>>. It receives a cancellation signal and returns the data or an error. The zero-argument Fn() -> Future shape, with the key and policies passed as separate arguments, belongs to use_query_unsignalled. The real networking is up to you (reqwest, an LSP transport, a local file). Here we return a fixed list so the example compiles without a server.

Call use_query in your view’s new. It returns a tuple: the resource entity (store it on the view to read during render) and a Subscription (store it too, because dropping it stops the view from re-rendering on changes).

use_query starts a fetch the first time the resource is seen, and reuses the cached entity on every subsequent access for the same key. Pass a fresh QueryKey (QueryKey::from(["todos", "list", "open"]) for a multi-segment key) when you want hierarchical keys for invalidation.

blocks.text: 4. Read status and data, then render

blocks.html: A QueryResource<T, E> is a normal GPUI entity. Read it with entity.read(cx) and branch on status():
Useful predicates on the resource:

items.html: r.is_loading(): true during the first fetch or any refetch.
r.is_pending(): true when there is no data yet (Idle, or the first load in progress).
r.data() / r.error(): Option<&T> / Option<&E>, borrowed for the duration of the read.

blocks.html: That is the whole query loop: define a fetcher, subscribe with use_query, branch on status, render. gpui-query handles caching, deduplication, and re-rendering on every status transition.

api/queries.title: Queries
api/queries.desc: use_query API reference for gpui-query: query keys, fetchers, cache and request policies, status handling, and reactive updates in GPUI components.

blocks.html: Queries are the core primitive. You define a key, a fetcher, and some options. The library handles caching, deduplication, retry, and reactive updates.

Every query produces an Entity<QueryResource<T, E>> that you read during render. Your component re-renders when the entity’s status changes or its data is replaced; same-status bookkeeping such as a retry counter increment does not trigger a render.

blocks.code:
fn use_query<T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    options: impl Into<QueryOptions>,
    fetcher: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
) -> (Entity<QueryResource<T, E>>, Subscription)
where
    F: Fn(QuerySignal) -> Fut + Send + 'static,
    Fut: Future<Output = Result<T, E>> + Send + 'static,

blocks.html: This is the primary hook. Call it in your component’s constructor, not in render. It gets or creates a QueryResource entity from the global QueryClient, sets up an observer that re-renders your component on status changes and data writes, and spawns an async fetch if the resource is idle.
The fetcher receives a QuerySignal for cooperative cancellation. Check signal.is_cancelled() periodically in long-running fetchers and abort early when possible.

Returns a tuple of (Entity<QueryResource<T, E>>, Subscription). Store the entity to read state during render. Store the subscription to keep the observation alive. Drop the subscription and the observation stops.
With options:
You can pass a &str, String, or QueryKey directly as the first argument because QueryOptions implements From for all three.

The QueryClient must be initialized before calling use_query. In debug builds, the hook panics if cx.set_global::<QueryClient>() was never called. In release builds, it falls back to a standalone entity with no shared caching or garbage collection.

blocks.code:
fn use_query_unsignalled<T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    key: QueryKey,
    cache_policy: CachePolicy,
    request_policy: RequestPolicy,
    fetcher: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
) -> (Entity<QueryResource<T, E>>, Subscription)
where
    F: Fn() -> Fut + Send + 'static,
    Fut: Future<Output = Result<T, E>> + Send + 'static,

blocks.html: The backward-compatible variant. The fetcher takes no signal argument: Fn() -> Fut instead of Fn(QuerySignal) -> Fut. This means your fetcher cannot observe cancellation.
Use this if you have existing fetch closures that do not need signal awareness. For new code, prefer use_query (the signal-accepting version).

Sets up the entity and observation without starting a fetch. Use this when you need full control over when and how fetching happens. A brand-new key starts in Idle status with no data; a key already live in the shared QueryClient (mounted elsewhere, for example) returns the existing entity with its current status and data.
You would call fetch_query or fetch_query_with_signal later to trigger a fetch on your own schedule.

blocks.code:
fn use_query_with_policy<T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    options: impl Into<QueryOptions>,
    fetcher: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
) -> (Entity<QueryResource<T, E>>, Subscription)
where
    F: Fn(QuerySignal) -> Fut + Send + 'static,
    Fut: Future<Output = Result<Fetched<T>, E>> + Send + 'static,

blocks.html: Like use_query, but the fetcher returns Result<Fetched<T>, E> instead of Result<T, E>. Everything else matches use_query.
Use this when a response carries its own caching directive that should override the caller’s per-query CachePolicy (“server wins”). On success, wrap your data in Fetched:

items.html: Fetched::new(data): keep the resource’s existing cache policy.
Fetched::with_policy(data, policy): replace the resource’s policy with the server’s, effective immediately after the fetch resolves. Subsequent freshness and SWR checks use the server’s TTL.

blocks.html: The plain Result<T, E> use_query is unchanged. Reach for use_query_with_policy only when the server can return a CachePolicy (typically HTTP APIs with Cache-Control / Expires headers).
See the HTTP caching guide for cache_policy_from_headers, and Caching: server wins with Fetched<T> for the full server-wins contract.

blocks.code:
fn fetch_query<T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    entity: &Entity<QueryResource<T, E>>,
    fetcher: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
) where
    F: Fn() -> Fut + Send + 'static,
    Fut: Future<Output = Result<T, E>> + Send + 'static,

blocks.html: Imperative refetch on an existing entity. The fetcher takes no signal. On failure, retries according to the entity’s retry policy.

The call always runs in QueryFetchMode::Normal, and so do fetch_query_with_signal and fetch_query_with_policy. It respects the entity’s cache policy and silently no-ops while the cached data is still fresh (default Ttl { ttl_ms: 60_000 }) or while a request is in flight under IgnoreWhileLoading. A fetch starts only once the cache policy allows it, or as a stale-while-revalidate background fetch. There is no forced variant, so a refresh button wired to fetch_query does nothing within the TTL.

blocks.code:
fn fetch_query_with_signal<T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    entity: &Entity<QueryResource<T, E>>,
    fetcher: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
) where
    F: FnOnce(QuerySignal) -> Fut + Send + 'static,
    Fut: Future<Output = Result<T, E>> + Send + 'static,

blocks.html: Like fetch_query, but the fetcher receives a QuerySignal. The fetcher signature is FnOnce(QuerySignal) -> Fut.
Because the closure is FnOnce, it is consumed on the first call. Retries are not possible. If you need retry logic, use fetch_query or use_query with a retry policy instead.

blocks.code:
fn fetch_query_with_policy<T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    entity: &Entity<QueryResource<T, E>>,
    fetcher: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
) where
    F: Fn() -> Fut + Send + 'static,
    Fut: Future<Output = Result<Fetched<T>, E>> + Send + 'static,

blocks.html: Like fetch_query, but the fetcher returns Result<Fetched<T>, E> so a server-derived CachePolicy can override the resource’s policy on success. The fetcher takes no signal, same as fetch_query. On failure, retries according to the entity’s retry policy.
Use this for imperative refetches whose response should update the cache policy, for example a manual refresh of an HTTP endpoint.
See use_query_with_policy for the server-wins contract, and the caching guide for details.

A cooperative cancellation token backed by Arc<AtomicBool>. Clones share the same underlying flag. When any clone calls cancel(), all clones observe is_cancelled() == true.
The library creates a fresh signal each time a fetch begins. The fetcher should check is_cancelled() periodically and abort early when possible.
Signals are cancelled automatically when a newer request replaces an older one (the LatestWins request policy), or when you call cancel() or reset() on the resource.
The default is Ttl { ttl_ms: 60_000 } (one minute).

items.html: NoCache: every mount triggers a fresh fetch.
Ttl: cached data is served if cache_age_ms is within ttl_ms. Once expired, a new fetch starts.

StaleWhileRevalidate: cached data is served fresh within ttl_ms. Between ttl_ms and ttl_ms + stale_ms, the stale data is served while a background refetch runs. Past ttl_ms + stale_ms, the data is expired and a normal fetch with a loading state runs.

blocks.html: See Caching for the full picture.
The default is LatestWins. Use IgnoreWhileLoading when you want to avoid redundant network traffic and the first response is good enough.

Set through QueryOptions::force(). Normal is the default. Force bypasses cache freshness checks and starts a new fetch, except under RequestPolicy::IgnoreWhileLoading: a request already in flight still blocks it, and the call returns IgnoredWhileLoading.

blocks.code:
let simple: QueryKey = QueryKey::from("users");
let compound: QueryKey = QueryKey::from(["users", "42", "posts"]);

blocks.html: Keys are hierarchical, modeled after TanStack Query’s array keys. Internally stored as Arc<[Arc<str>]>, so cloning is a single atomic ref-count increment.

Two operations use this structure: exact match for cache lookups, and prefix match via starts_with() for cache invalidation. A key like ["users", "42"] matches the prefix ["users"] but not ["users", "43"].
QueryKey implements From<&str>, From<String>, From<[&str; N]>, From<Vec<&str>>, and From<Vec<String>>.

api/mutations.title: Mutations
api/mutations.desc: use_mutation API reference for gpui-query: dispatching writes from GPUI components, success and error callbacks, and coordinating cache invalidation.

blocks.html: Mutations handle write operations: creating a user, updating a record, deleting a resource. Unlike Queries, mutations don’t run automatically. You trigger them explicitly, and they manage their own loading/success/failure lifecycle.

A mutation does not touch the query cache on its own. If you need to invalidate or refetch queries after a mutation succeeds, do that in an on_success callback. The library doesn’t guess which queries a mutation should affect.

blocks.code:
pub fn use_mutation<V, T, E, C>(
    options: impl Into<MutationOptions>,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
) -> (Entity<MutationResource<V, T, E>>, Subscription)

blocks.html: Creates a new MutationResource entity and returns it together with the Subscription that keeps its observer alive; store both on your view struct. The entity starts in the Idle state: pass () for the default retry behavior (no retries) or a MutationOptions to change it. use_mutation reads only retry_policy from the options; mutation garbage collection is governed by the QueryClient global’s GC time (default 5 minutes, set with QueryClient::with_gc_time). Read from the entity during render to show loading spinners, error messages, or success state.
The returned entity is a GPUI Entity, so you observe it like any other entity: call entity.read(cx) to inspect status, data, and error fields during render.

blocks.code:
pub fn mutate<V, T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    entity: &Entity<MutationResource<V, T, E>>,
    variables: V,
    mutator: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
)

blocks.html: Triggers a mutation on the entity. It transitions the resource to Loading, spawns an async task running your mutator closure, and handles the outcome (including retries if the entity has a retry policy).

The mutator closure receives the variables and must return a Future<Output = Result<T, E>>. A call while the entity is already loading is ignored. Otherwise it stores the new variables, clears the error, and resets the retry count; previous success data stays readable until the new attempt settles (replaced on success, cleared on failure or cancel).
mutate holds a WeakEntity reference internally, so dropping the entity before the async task finishes is safe. The task exits.

A call made while the entity is still Loading is a no-op: the built-in is_loading() guard ignores it and the in-flight mutation keeps running. You don’t need a manual entity.read(cx).is_loading() check to prevent concurrent mutations. mutate_with_callbacks, mutate_by_ref, and mutate_arc behave the same way.

blocks.code:
pub fn mutate_with_callbacks<V, T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    entity: &Entity<MutationResource<V, T, E>>,
    variables: V,
    mutator: F,
    callbacks: MutationCallbacks<T, E>,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
)

blocks.html: Identical to mutate but accepts a MutationCallbacks struct that fires on the final outcome. Callbacks run on the terminal outcome: first success, exhausted retries, or a mutation ended early by cancel(), reset(), or the entity being dropped. They do not fire on intermediate retry attempts.
This is where you invalidate query caches after a successful write:
See the MutationCallbacks section for the full callback API.

blocks.code:
pub fn mutate_by_ref<V, T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    entity: &Entity<MutationResource<V, T, E>>,
    variables: V,
    mutator: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,
)

blocks.html: Same trigger as mutate, but the mutator receives &V borrowed from the stored Arc<V>, so there is no V::clone per attempt. V: Clone is still required, because begin stores an owned copy.
The returned future must be 'static, so clone what you need out of vars before the async move block.

blocks.code:
pub fn mutate_arc<V, T, E, C, F, Fut>(
    entity: &Entity<MutationResource<V, T, E>>,
    variables: Arc<V>,
    mutator: F,
    cx: &mut Context<C>,

blocks.html: mutate_by_ref taking Arc<V> directly, so callers can share one variables buffer across calls. Both variants take the same Fn(&V) mutator, and neither accepts MutationCallbacks.

blocks.code: pub fn use_mutation_state<V, T, E, C>(cx: &mut Context<C>) -> Vec<Entity<MutationResource<V, T, E>>>

blocks.html: Returns a snapshot of all MutationResource entities matching the (V, T, E) type triple registered in the global QueryClient. Useful for devtools or status bars that need to observe all mutations of a particular kind across the entire app.
Returns an empty Vec if no mutations exist for that type triple or if no QueryClient is set up.
The core state container for a single mutation. Three type parameters:

items.html: V is the variables (input) type. What you pass into the mutation.
T is the success output type. The data returned on completion.
E is the error type. Defaults to QueryError.

blocks.html: Every mutation goes through these states in order:

items.html: Idle: initial state. No mutation has been triggered.
Loading: begin(variables) was called. The variables are stored, the error is cleared, and a fresh cancellation signal is created.
Success or Failure: the async task completes. complete_success(data) stores the result and clears the error. complete_failure(error) stores the error and increments the retry counter.

blocks.html: If the entity has a retry policy and retries remain after a failure, the internal loop keeps the mutation in Loading via increment_retry() and prepare_retry() (observers never see a transient Failure between attempts) and runs the mutator again. complete_failure() runs only when retries are exhausted. retry() is a public manual Failure to Loading helper, not what the loop uses.

The loop calls reset_retry_count() right after the terminal complete_success and complete_failure, undoing complete_failure’s increment. A mutation driven through mutate or any of its variants always reads retry_count() == 0 once settled; the counter is non-zero only mid-flight between retry attempts, or when you drive the resource by hand.

blocks.html: is_idle(), is_loading(), is_success(), is_failure() each return bool. These are convenience wrappers around status() checks.
begin(variables) transitions to Loading. Stores the variables, clears any previous error and the GC timestamp, resets the retry count, and creates a fresh QuerySignal.
complete_success(data) transitions to Success. Stores the result data and clears the signal.
complete_failure(error) transitions to Failure. Stores the error, increments retry_count, and clears the signal.
should_retry() -> bool checks whether retry_count < max_retries according to the retry policy.

retry() -> bool attempts to transition from Failure back to Loading. Only succeeds when should_retry() is true and the current status is Failure. Preserves the original variables and creates a fresh signal. Returns true if the retry was initiated.

cancel(error) only acts while the status is Loading: it sets Failure with the given error, clears stored data, increments cancelled_count, and cancels the signal so in-flight async work can observe it. In any other status it returns without changing state.
reset() returns the resource to Idle and clears everything: data, error, variables, retry count, cancelled count, signal, and timestamp.
with_key(key) associates a QueryKey with this mutation for cache correlation. Returns self for builder-style chaining.
Each variant has a label() method returning a &'static str ("Idle", "Loading", "Success", "Failure").

A struct of optional closures that fire when a mutation settles. Construct it with the builder pattern:

Each field is an Option<Arc<...>>: on_success is Option<Arc<dyn Fn(&T) + Send + Sync>>, on_error is Option<Arc<dyn Fn(&E) + Send + Sync>>, and on_settled is Option<Arc<dyn Fn(Option<&T>, Option<&E>) + Send + Sync>>. api/infinite-queries.title: Infinite Queries
api/infinite-queries.desc: use_infinite_query API reference for gpui-query: bidirectional page fetching, max_pages limits, and rendering paginated data in GPUI components.

blocks.html: Infinite queries handle paginated data: feed streams, cursor-based lists, any scenario where you load a chunk at a time and might need more later. The API is modeled after TanStack Query’s useInfiniteQuery, adapted to GPUI’s synchronous rendering model and Rust’s ownership semantics.

The hook returns two things: an Entity<InfiniteQueryResource<T, E>> holding all loaded pages, and a Subscription that keeps the observation alive. Drop the subscription and the view stops re-rendering on state changes.

The fetcher closure receives Option<&T> (the last page for forward fetches, the first page for backward fetches, or None on the initial request). It returns Result<(T, bool), E> where the bool tells the query whether more pages exist.
On creation, the hook starts an initial fetch if the resource is idle. The entity is registered with QueryClient for shared caching and garbage collection.
Call this from event handlers to load the next page. Common trigger: the user scrolled to the bottom of a list.
The function reads the last page from the entity and passes it to your fetcher. It returns nothing; the entity updates in place and the view re-renders when the fetch completes.
If has_next_page() is false, the call does nothing. If a fetch is already in flight under RequestPolicy::LatestWins, the old request is cancelled and replaced.
Same shape as fetch_next_page_infinite, but fetches in the backward direction. The fetcher receives the first page (not the last) so you can compute a cursor for older content.

This is useful for chat interfaces or timelines that grow in both directions. has_previous_page starts false in both directions, so setting FetchDirection::Bidirectional does not by itself enable backward fetching. Each page is stored as one Arc<T>, so first_page_arc() and last_page_arc() hand you a page with a refcount bump instead of a copy.

The _with_id variants accept a pre-allocated RequestId from the QueryClient bucket’s sequencer to maintain monotonic IDs across the resource’s lifetime. Passing None to a _with_id variant falls back to an internal sequencer stored on the resource (transient_sequencer), so a bare begin_fetch_next_with_id(None, now_ms) mints its own ID.

Bidirectional sets both to false. The query will not fetch in either direction until you explicitly call set_has_next_page(true) or set_has_previous_page(true), or until a successful fetch returns has_more = true.

This matters under RequestPolicy::LatestWins. When a user scrolls fast and triggers multiple fetches, each new fetch cancels the previous one. Late-arriving responses from cancelled fetches are silently dropped.

api/query-client.title: QueryClient
api/query-client.desc: QueryClient API reference for gpui-query: the global registry that owns query resources, garbage collection, invalidation, and cache persistence.

blocks.html: QueryClient is a GPUI Global that holds every query, infinite query, and mutation entity in your application. You set it up once during app initialization and access it from any GPUI context through cx.global::<QueryClient>().

QueryClient::new() takes no arguments. The default policies are already CachePolicy::Ttl { ttl_ms: 60_000 } and RequestPolicy::LatestWins; use QueryClient::with_policies(cache_policy, request_policy) when you want different defaults. Every query resource created through resource() inherits these unless you override them per-resource. The client holds no default retry policy: mutation retries are set per resource with MutationOptions::retry_policy (default no_retries()) passed to use_mutation.

head: Method
Description
rows: Create a client with the default policies (Ttl { ttl_ms: 60_000 }, LatestWins)
Create a client with custom default policies
Set the garbage-collection age cutoff: idle resources older than this are collected (default: 300,000 ms; Success resources survive twice as long, values below 1,000 ms are clamped)

blocks.html: Get or create a QueryResource<T, E> entity for the given key. The key is generic: &str, String, [&str; N], Vec<&str>, Vec<String>, and QueryKey all convert. If a resource already exists for that key and type pair, it returns the existing entity. Otherwise it creates a new one with the client’s default policies.

blocks.html: Read-only lookup: return the existing resource for the given key and type pair, or None if none exists. Creates nothing.

blocks.html: Return all query entities for a specific (T, E) type pair. Returns an empty vec if no bucket exists for that type.

blocks.html: Clone the stored data for the given key. Returns None if no resource exists for the key, the entity was collected, or the resource has not completed a fetch.
Zero-clone counterpart to get_query_data: f receives &T for the duration of the call. Same None conditions.

Imperatively begin a fetch. Creates the resource if needed, then starts a request that always runs in Force mode, so it never short-circuits on a fresh cache and no separate force variant exists. Returns None only when the request policy ignored the start (IgnoreWhileLoading). No observer is attached.

The returned PreparedFetch carries the public fields entity, request_id, and signal (an owned QuerySignal). Run your async fetcher with the signal, then complete the request via prepared.complete_success(data, cx) or prepared.complete_failure(e, cx).

For refetches on an entity that already has an observer attached, use the hook-layer free function gpui_query::fetch_query(entity, fetcher, cx) (plus fetch_query_with_policy and fetch_query_with_signal).

blocks.html: Prefetch a query in the background. T and E require Clone + Send + Sync + 'static; the timestamp is captured internally, so there is no now_ms parameter. None means a fresh cache hit (read the cached value via get_query_data) or that the request policy ignored the start. Some(prepared) binds the request: run your async fetcher with prepared.signal and complete it via prepared.complete_success(data, cx) / prepared.complete_failure(e, cx). Useful for warming the cache before a user navigates to a new view.

blocks.html: Set data on a resource without completing a request. The resource is created if it does not exist, and the previous data is kept so a later write can restore it. Observers are notified and the persist snapshot is marked dirty.
Use this for optimistic updates: update the cache immediately, then let the mutation result or a refetch correct it later.

QueryClient has no dedicated rollback method. Capture the previous value with get_query_data (returns None when no data is stored) before the optimistic write, then restore it with set_query_data if the mutation fails:

set_query_data notifies observers, so mounted views re-render with the restored data and the persist driver saves the change. Calling rollback_to_previous() on the resource entity restores the same value but does not notify observers.
Bulk operations use QueryKeyFilter to target resources across all type-partitioned buckets. They work on every (T, E) type pair at once.
Prefix is useful for invalidating all queries under a namespace. For example, Prefix(&QueryKey::from(["users"])) matches ["users", "42"], ["users", "42", "posts"], and so on.

blocks.html: Mark matching resources as stale by clearing their cache freshness. Does not cancel active requests. The next time a stale resource is accessed, it will trigger a refetch.

blocks.html: Clear data and error state on matching resources, resetting them to idle while keeping the entity registered. Each resource’s in-flight signal is cancelled, so cooperative fetchers abort early and late results are ignored. Contrast invalidate_queries, which only clears cache freshness and leaves active requests running.

blocks.html: Remove matching resources from the registry entirely. This drops each registry entry, the weak entity reference and its co-located sequencer; an entity still held by a mounted view through a strong Entity handle survives until its last handle is released. Unlike reset_queries, removed keys are no longer registered, and accessing one again creates the resource fresh with a new sequencer. Only query and infinite-query buckets are swept; mutation buckets are left untouched.

blocks.code:
// Remove everything
client.remove_queries(&QueryKeyFilter::All);
fn cancel_queries(&mut self, filter: &QueryKeyFilter, cx: &mut App)

blocks.html: Cancel the in-flight signal of matching loading requests and ignore their late results. No QueryError::cancelled error is set; the resource’s status and error are left untouched. Use QueryKeyFilter::Exact(&key) to cancel a single key.

blocks.html: Register an already-created mutation entity in the client’s (V, T, E) bucket. The three type parameters are: V (variables/input), T (success result), and E (error type). use_mutation calls this automatically, so you rarely call it by hand. The retry policy is set per mutation through MutationOptions (default no retries, override with .retry_policy(...)), not by the client.

blocks.html: Return all mutation entities for a specific (V, T, E) type triple. Returns an empty vec if no mutations of that type exist.

blocks.html: Collect idle query and mutation resources older than the client’s gc_time_ms, reading the clock itself. Resources with active requests are never collected: Loading mutations always survive, Success mutations survive twice the gc time, and Idle/Failure mutations survive the gc time (floored at 1 second during GC). There is no separate mutation GC pass; gc sweeps mutation buckets too. Call this periodically (every 30 seconds is reasonable).

let client = cx.global_mut::<QueryClient>();
client.gc(cx);

blocks.html: Same sweep with a caller-supplied timestamp, for when you already hold a time value.

blocks.html: Return a Clone + Debug snapshot of the entire client state as plain data structs; implement your own serialization or logging on top. Useful for devtools panels or logging. This is the only diagnostics entry point on QueryClient; per-type and per-bucket counts are not exposed.

blocks.html: Rust’s type system treats Entity<QueryResource<User>> and Entity<QueryResource<Post>> as different types. You cannot store them in the same HashMap. QueryClient solves this by partitioning resources into type-specific buckets keyed by TypeId of (T, E).

Each bucket is stored as a type-erased Box<dyn ErasedBucket> trait object keyed by TypeId of (T, E); mutation buckets use the analogous ErasedMutationBucket. Both erased traits are crate-private implementation details, not public API. Bulk operations like invalidate_queries iterate across all buckets through the trait, without needing to know the concrete types. Typed access methods like resource::<User, MyError>() downcast to the correct bucket.
This means invalidate_queries with QueryKeyFilter::All will touch every query regardless of its data type, which is usually what you want after a logout or a global state reset.

guides/caching.title: Caching
guides/caching.desc: Configure caching in gpui-query: how NoCache, Ttl, and StaleWhileRevalidate policies decide when data is fresh, stale, or refetched in the background.

blocks.html: Every query in gpui-query has a cache policy. The policy determines whether a fetch happens at all, and whether stale data gets served while a refetch runs in the background. Picking a policy is how you trade data freshness against request volume.
There are three variants of CachePolicy. The default is Ttl { ttl_ms: 60_000 }, a 60-second TTL. You can override it per query or set a different default when constructing the QueryClient.

blocks.code: CachePolicy::NoCache

blocks.html: Every access triggers a fresh fetch. Data from a successful fetch is stored on the resource, but never served as a cache hit on a later access. Use this for data that changes constantly and where showing a stale value is worse than showing nothing.
The practical effect: begin_request never returns CacheHit. Under IgnoreWhileLoading with a request already in flight it still returns IgnoredWhileLoading.

blocks.code: CachePolicy::Ttl { ttl_ms: 30_000 }

blocks.html: Data is fresh for ttl_ms milliseconds after it was last fetched. While fresh, accessing the query returns CacheHit and skips the network entirely. After the TTL expires, the next access starts a new fetch.
This is the default policy.

blocks.code: CachePolicy::StaleWhileRevalidate { ttl_ms: 30_000, stale_ms: 60_000 }

blocks.html: This policy splits the cache lifetime into two windows.
Fresh window (0 to ttl_ms): data is served from cache. No fetch happens. Same as Ttl.
Stale window (ttl_ms to ttl_ms + stale_ms): cached data is returned immediately, and a background refetch starts. The caller gets StaleCacheHit with a request_id for the background fetch.
Expired (past ttl_ms + stale_ms): the data is too old to serve. A normal fetch happens, same as a cache miss.
Use this when your UI benefits from showing slightly outdated data rather than flashing a loading spinner. Feed timelines, dashboards, and list views are common candidates.
CachePolicy exposes six methods that control the caching decision internally. You normally do not call these yourself (the library does).

items.html: is_fresh(age_ms) - returns true when age_ms is within the TTL window
is_stale_but_serveable(age_ms) - returns true when the age is past TTL but within the stale window (only StaleWhileRevalidate)
is_expired(age_ms) - returns true when the age exceeds the total valid window. NoCache always returns true
can_short_circuit() - whether the policy can ever skip a fetch (true for Ttl and StaleWhileRevalidate; a pure policy check with no freshness condition)
can_serve_stale() - whether stale data can be served (true only for StaleWhileRevalidate)
total_valid_ms() - returns ttl_ms + stale_ms for SWR, ttl_ms for Ttl, None for NoCache

blocks.html: The freshness half of those two decisions lives in the resource: should_short_circuit_cache(now_ms) and should_serve_stale_and_revalidate(now_ms) combine the policy checks with the age of the data.
Pass the policy when creating a QueryClient to set the app-wide default.
Override per query through QueryOptions:

blocks.code:
let opts = QueryOptions::new(QueryKey::from(["notifications"]))
    .cache_policy(CachePolicy::NoCache);

blocks.html: Or use resource_with_policies on the client directly:
When multiple parts of your app request the same key at the same time, the RequestPolicy decides what happens.
A new request cancels the in-flight one and starts fresh. This is the right choice when you always want the most recent data and do not care about wasting the earlier request.

blocks.code: RequestPolicy::LatestWins

blocks.html: If a request is already in progress, new requests for the same key are ignored. The original request runs to completion. Use this when fetches are idempotent and you want to avoid redundant work.

blocks.code: RequestPolicy::IgnoreWhileLoading

blocks.html: When you call begin_request on a resource, the return value tells you what happened.

items.html: Started - a new fetch was kicked off. replaced_request_id is Some if this request cancelled a previous one (under LatestWins).
CacheHit - the cache is fresh, no fetch needed. Use the cached data.
StaleCacheHit - data is stale but still serveable. Return the stale data to the UI immediately, then use the request_id to run a background fetch.
IgnoredWhileLoading - a request was already running and the policy is IgnoreWhileLoading.

blocks.html: QueryFetchMode controls whether the cache is consulted.

items.html: Normal (default) - respects the cache policy. Returns CacheHit if fresh.
Force - bypasses cache freshness. Always starts a new fetch. Still respects IgnoreWhileLoading if a request is already in flight.

blocks.html: Use Force when a query’s first fetch must bypass freshness checks. The hooks only fetch from Idle, so forcing a query that is already Success starts nothing. For pull-to-refresh or a manual reload button, drive the fetch yourself with prepare_fetch_query (below).

For a manual forced fetch outside the hooks, client.prepare_fetch_query::<UserData, MyError>(key, cx) takes only the key and cx, runs with the client’s default policies, and returns Option<PreparedFetch<T, E>>. It returns None when IgnoreWhileLoading defers to a request already in flight.
The QueryClient has bulk methods that operate across all resources matching a filter. These use QueryKeyFilter to select which queries to touch.
invalidate_queries clears cache freshness on matching resources. The next access to those queries will trigger a refetch. It does not cancel in-flight requests.
This is the standard pattern after a mutation: invalidate the affected query prefix so the next read fetches fresh data.

remove_queries drops matching resources from the registry entirely. Unlike invalidation, which keeps the entity and expires its cache, removal deletes the registry entry only; the entity itself stays alive until the last strong handle elsewhere (such as a view holding the Entity returned by use_query) is dropped.

blocks.code: client.remove_queries(&QueryKeyFilter::All);

items.html: Exact(&key) - matches only the exact key
Prefix(&key) - matches all keys that start with the given prefix segments
All - matches every key

blocks.html: Prefix matching is hierarchical. Prefix(&QueryKey::from(["users"])) matches ["users"], ["users", "42"], and ["users", "42", "posts"].
Sometimes you want to update the UI before the server confirms the change. set_query_data writes a value directly into the cache, storing the previous value for rollback.
QueryClient has no dedicated rollback method. Capture the previous value with get_query_data before the optimistic write, then restore it if the mutation fails:

Restoring through set_query_data notifies observers and marks the persist snapshot, so mounted views re-render and the rollback is persisted. Calling rollback_to_previous() on the resource entity restores the same value but does not notify observers.

Buckets hold only weak entity handles, so a query no component is observing has its resource freed by GPUI refcounting as soon as the last handle drops; garbage collection then prunes the leftover registry entries. The gc method on QueryClient collects Idle, Failure, and Cancelled resources that have been idle longer than gc_time_ms (clamped to a 1 second floor), keeps Success resources for twice that or as long as a stale-while-revalidate policy can still serve them, and never collects a resource with a fetch in flight.

blocks.code:
let client = cx.global_mut::<QueryClient>();
client.gc(cx);

blocks.html: If you already hold a timestamp, client.gc_with_time(now_ms, cx) skips the clock read.

The default GC time is 5 minutes (300,000 ms), and it is a client-wide setting: change it with QueryClient::with_gc_time. The gc_time_ms field on QueryOptions, written through the .gc_time() builder, is reserved and has no effect today.
A fetcher normally returns Result<T, E>, and the resource uses whatever CachePolicy the caller supplied through QueryOptions. That policy is decided entirely on the client.

Sometimes the server knows better. A Cache-Control: max-age=30 response header is more authoritative than a TTL you guessed at compile time. The *_with_policy hooks let a fetcher return Result<Fetched<T>, E> instead, carrying a server-derived CachePolicy that overrides the caller’s per-query policy once the fetch resolves successfully.

items.html: use_query_with_policy(options, fetcher, cx) - same shape as use_query (options-first, signal-accepting fetcher, returns (Entity<QueryResource<T, E>>, Subscription)), but the fetcher returns Result<Fetched<T>, E>.
fetch_query_with_policy(&entity, fetcher, cx) - same shape as fetch_query, but the fetcher returns Result<Fetched<T>, E>.

blocks.html: Fetched<T> has three constructors:
A fetcher that parses only the response headers can push that TTL back into the resource:

The server policy replaces the resource’s stored policy immediately after complete_success, so subsequent freshness and SWR checks use the server’s TTL. Returning Fetched::new(data) (or using the plain Result<T, E> hooks) leaves the caller’s policy untouched. Server-wins is strictly opt-in.

Fetched::with_meta requires the persist feature. The opaque meta flows into PersistedEntry::meta when the resource is persisted, so it survives a cold start. See Persistence. For the full HTTP Cache-Control and ETag flow, see HTTP caching.
A typical setup looks like this:
Then override per query as needed. A real-time notifications feed might use NoCache. A rarely-changing config endpoint might use Ttl { ttl_ms: 300_000 }.
See Queries for how to define queries that use these policies, QueryClient for the full client API, and Error Handling for what happens when a fetch fails.

guides/error-handling.title: Error handling
guides/error-handling.desc: Handle query errors in gpui-query: the error status lifecycle, retries with backoff, cooperative cancellation, and rendering failures in GPUI views.

blocks.html: Queries fail. Networks drop, servers return 500, users go offline. gpui-query tracks errors as part of the resource state so your UI can respond to them without extra bookkeeping.
Every query and mutation uses QueryError as the default error type. It wraps two fields: a QueryErrorKind and a message string.
The four variants of QueryErrorKind are:

items.html: Response for server-side errors (HTTP 4xx/5xx, application-level rejections)
Transport for network failures, timeouts, DNS errors
Cancelled for cooperative cancellation (a superseding request under LatestWins, a reset, or cancel_queries)
Unknown for anything that does not fit the above

blocks.html: Each variant has a constructor helper so you do not spell out the kind explicitly:
QueryError implements std::fmt::Display and std::error::Error. The display format is "{kind}: {message}", so it prints cleanly in logs and works with the ? operator:
Because it implements std::error::Error, you can also return it through anyhow:
Internally the message uses Arc<str>, so cloning a QueryError is a pointer bump. This matters in high-retry scenarios where the same error ends up stored in multiple locations.
Error messages often contain data you do not want in logs: database credentials, file paths, auth tokens. QueryError::sanitized() returns a new QueryError with known sensitive patterns redacted:
It handles these patterns:

items.html: Connection strings: postgres://..., postgresql://..., mysql://..., mysql2://..., mongodb://..., mongodb+srv://..., redis://..., rediss://..., amqp://..., mssql://...
Bearer tokens and token assignments: Bearer ..., token=...
File paths: /home/..., /users/..., /etc/..., /var/..., plus the same segments with Windows backslashes (\home\..., \users\..., \etc\..., \var\...)
Email addresses
Long hex sequences (16+ hex chars, likely API keys or secrets)

blocks.html: Messages longer than 512 bytes get truncated at the nearest preceding char boundary, with ...[truncated] appended. The kind is preserved, only the message changes.
The sanitization runs a scan without depending on the regex crate. The connection and path needles match ASCII case-insensitively, so /Users/... redacts too.
When a query fails, the error is stored on the QueryResource. Read it inside read_with:
The error() method returns Option<&E>. It is Some whenever the resource is in a failure state. You can also check the kind to branch your UI:
QueryStatus has three states relevant to errors:

items.html: Failure means the query completed with an error. error() will return Some.

LoadingWithData means a fetch is in progress while data from an earlier fetch is still available via data(). Any fetch that starts with existing data enters this state, typically a refetch or a background revalidation, and the previous error is cleared at that moment, so no prior failure is implied. This is the “show old data while refetching” scenario.

Cancelled means an explicit cancel() was called on the resource with an error attached. A new query with the same key superseding the current one does not produce this state: the resource moves straight into the new request’s loading state and the superseded fetch’s result is dropped.

blocks.html: When a refetch fails, gpui-query keeps the last successful data around. You can show it to the user while also surfacing the error:
MutationResource<V, T, E> tracks errors the same way. After a mutation fails, status() returns MutationStatus::Failure and error() returns the error:

Mutations also track a retry count. Call should_retry() to check whether the retry policy allows another attempt, then call retry() to transition back to Loading. See Retry for the full retry configuration.
Sanitize before logging. Any error that leaves your app (logs, analytics, crash reporting) should go through sanitized().

Check has_data() alongside error(). A resource can have both data and an error at the same time (the Failure state, which keeps the previous data; LoadingWithData always has its error cleared on entry). If you only check error(), you might hide good data that is still valid to show.
Match on QueryErrorKind to decide what to show. Transport errors warrant a different UI response than server errors. Cancelled errors usually do not need to be shown at all.
For retry configuration, see the Retry guide. For the full query and mutation API, see Queries and Mutations.

guides/retry.title: Retry
guides/retry.desc: Configure automatic retries in gpui-query: fixed and exponential backoff RetryPolicy options, caps, and how retries interact with cancellation.

blocks.html: Failed fetches are retried automatically. A RetryPolicy says how many times to retry, how long to wait between attempts, and whether to back off exponentially. Queries and mutations share the same policy type but start from different defaults.

Queries default to retry because transient network failures are common and the user did not ask for the fetch, so silently retrying is the friendlier behavior. Mutations default to no retries because they are user-initiated and often destructive; silently re-running a “create” or “delete” on failure can duplicate or destroy data. Opt into mutation retry explicitly when you know it is safe.
RetryPolicy is Clone + Debug + Serialize + Deserialize. Build one with the constructor and the chained builders:

On a mutation, set it through MutationOptions::retry_policy:
You can also change a policy on an existing QueryResource at runtime via set_retry_policy, or read the active one with retry_policy().
delay_for_attempt(attempt) returns the delay before the attempt at the given 0-based index:

items.html: Without exponential backoff: every delay is retry_delay_ms. Five retries at 500ms wait 500ms each.

With exponential backoff: delay is retry_delay_ms * 2^attempt, capped first by max_retry_delay_ms and then by a hard ceiling of one hour. The shift is itself capped at 62 so the factor never overflows.

blocks.html: should_retry(current_retries) returns true while current_retries < max_retries. That is the condition the resource loop checks to decide whether to schedule another attempt.

While the resource is between the initial failure and either a successful retry or exhausted retries, the status stays Loading (specifically LoadingEmpty on first load or LoadingWithData on a refetch). The retry counter increments via increment_retry(), but because the QueryObserver deduplicates by status, your view does not re-render on every retry tick, only on the terminal outcome (Success or Failure).

This is the reason retry can be aggressive by default without thrashing the UI: three retries with exponential backoff look like one loading state to the user, with the spinner shown until the request either succeeds or the policy is exhausted.

A retry in progress is cancelled if a newer request supersedes it (LatestWins) or the resource is reset/unmounted. After the retry delay the loop re-checks whether the request is still the current one; only then does it increment the retry counter and hand the next attempt a fresh signal, so a superseded fetch wastes no attempt. A superseded or reset retry surfaces nothing: the loop stops without writing a status or an error. QueryStatus::Cancelled and QueryErrorKind::Cancelled appear only when something calls cancel() explicitly. See Error handling: Error states in QueryStatus.

items.html: Non-idempotent mutations. A POST /charge that fails after the request was sent but before the response arrived may have already charged the card. Retrying can double-charge. Keep the no_retries default for these.
4xx errors. A 400 or 401 will not succeed on retry; it burns the retry budget and delays surfacing the real error. Map these to QueryError::response and consider a policy with fewer retries.
User-visible destructive actions. Let the user decide whether to retry, so they stay in control of side effects.

blocks.html: Retry is most useful for transient failures: network blips, 5xx responses, timeouts. For these, exponential backoff with an appropriate cap is usually the right call.

items.html: Error handling: how retries and QueryError interact.
Caching: what triggers a fetch in the first place.
Queries / Mutations: where retry policies attach.

guides/persistence.title: Persistence
guides/persistence.desc: Save and restore cached query data across app restarts with the async Persister trait, persist_with, and hydrate.

blocks.html: Persistence lets your app start with data already in the cache instead of an empty loading state. Enable the persist feature and gpui-query drives a snapshot of your Success entries through an async backend you implement (the filesystem, a database, or a KV store). It saves on a debounce and restores on cold start.
Persistence is gated behind the persist feature. Add it alongside hook:

blocks.code: gpui-query = { version = "0.3.1", features = ["hook", "persist"] }

blocks.html: The cache stores type-erased buckets, so persistence has to move typed data (Vec<User>, Config, …) through an opaque shape. gpui-query splits that into seven pieces:

head: Piece
Role
rows: Async trait you implement: load() -> Result<PersistSnapshot, PersistError> and save(&PersistSnapshot) -> Result<(), PersistError>.
The on-wire shape: a map of key → { value (JSON), cached_at, cache_policy, meta }.

A debounced driver that reacts to cache mutations, collecting one snapshot per debounce window (bursts coalesce into a single save of the latest state) and handing it to the persister. Returns a PersistHandle drop-guard.
Cold-start restore: load a snapshot and re-prime the live cache.
Typed T -> JSON and JSON -> T conversions; serializers keyed by T, deserializers are unkeyed steps that hydrate tries in registration order. Required for the value-carrying round-trip.
Tuning: which keys (Exact / Prefix / All), max age, debounce.
Typed errors; the snapshot format version loaders check.

blocks.html: Only resources whose data type T has a registered serializer are emitted, and only types with a registered deserializer come back on hydrate. Register both. Serializers are keyed by the concrete T alone: registering the same T under two error types overwrites the first, and the surviving closure applies to every (T, E) bucket. Deserializers are not keyed at all; each registration appends a step, and hydrate offers every on-disk entry to every step in registration order. The E in register_deserializer only picks the bucket that gets primed on success:

hydrate offers every on-disk entry to every registered deserializer. There is no type tag on PersistedEntry, so routing is by trial. A deserializer must return None for any shape that is not its own, or a foreign entry can be mis-primed. Keep them strict and cheap.

Persister is async and Send + Sync + 'static; the save future runs on GPUI’s background executor, so blocking I/O is fine there. Be tolerant on load. A missing or corrupt store should yield an empty snapshot, not an error:
For tests or a disabled mode, NoopPersister persists nothing and loads an empty snapshot.

QueryClient::persist_with(persister, opts, cx) observes cache mutations and, after a short debounce, collects a fresh snapshot and calls persister.save. Bursts coalesce into one save per window. It returns a PersistHandle. Hold it for as long as you want saves to continue; dropping it stops scheduling new saves (one save already waiting on its timer may still finish).
For a one-shot snapshot without the driver, call client.collect_persist_snapshot(&filter, max_age, cx) and persist it yourself.
The free hydrate function loads a snapshot and re-primes the live cache through the registered deserializers. Call it once during startup, before your views mount.
Entries older than max_age, excluded by filter, or without a matching deserializer are skipped. A snapshot whose version does not match PERSIST_VERSION returns PersistError::VersionMismatch.
The companion crate gpui-query-persist ships a disk adapter, so you usually do not implement Persister yourself:

blocks.code: cargo add gpui-query-persist

blocks.html: Each save is atomic and durable: it writes a sibling temp file, fsyncs it (issuing F_FULLFSYNC on macOS), renames it over the target, and fsyncs the parent directory on POSIX, so a crash mid-write never leaves a corrupt cache. Loading is tolerant: a missing file yields an empty snapshot, a corrupt file is logged and treated as empty, and a version mismatch surfaces as a typed PersistError::VersionMismatch.

If you fetch over HTTP, you can attach opaque metadata to a fetched value with Fetched::with_meta. It lands in PersistedEntry::meta and round-trips back through persistence. That lets you issue cheap 304 refetches after relaunch. See HTTP cache headers.

items.html: On app shutdown: the simplest correct strategy. persist_with’s debounce lands a final flush shortly after the last mutation; drop the handle on quit.
Continuously, debounced: for long-running apps that may be killed without a clean shutdown. The default 500ms debounce keeps write volume bounded.
Scoped: use PersistFilter::Prefix to persist only a subtree (e.g. user data, not ephemeral feed pages).

blocks.html: Sanitize errors before they reach persistence. A QueryError built from a raw server response can carry tokens or connection strings. See Error handling: Error sanitization.

items.html: HTTP cache headers: derive a CachePolicy from Cache-Control and persist ETags.
Caching: how CachePolicy travels with each persisted entry.
Query keys: keys are what make a restored entry addressable.

guides/http-caching.title: HTTP cache headers
guides/http-caching.desc: Turn a server's Cache-Control into a gpui-query CachePolicy (server wins) and persist ETags for cheap 304 refetches with gpui-query-http.

blocks.html: The companion crate gpui-query-http turns your server’s HTTP cache headers into a gpui-query CachePolicy. Two pieces: a parser that derives the policy from response headers, and an in-memory HttpCache you can layer over any HTTP client. The server drives cache TTLs, and a relaunch refetch can be a cheap 304 Not Modified.

blocks.code: cargo add gpui-query-http

blocks.html: A fetcher normally returns Result<T, E> and the resource keeps whatever CachePolicy the caller asked for. When the server knows better (it sent Cache-Control: max-age=30, after all), return Result<Fetched<T>, E> from a *_with_policy hook and the server’s policy overrides the caller’s on success.
Parse the response headers with cache_policy_from_headers, hand the result to Fetched::with_policy, and consume the resource with use_query_with_policy:

The resource adopts the server’s TTL for as long as that value is fresh. use_query_with_policy is the server-wins variant of use_query; on refetch, fetch_query_with_policy reapplies the same override.

If cache_policy_from_headers returns an error (a malformed max-age), fall back to CachePolicy::NoCache rather than surfacing the parse error to the user. A no-store response is never an error; it maps cleanly to NoCache.
cache_policy_from_headers(headers: &http::HeaderMap) -> Result<CachePolicy, ParseError> reads Cache-Control per [RFC 9111]. Rules, in priority order:

items.html: Cache-Control: no-store or no-cache (bare or any value) → CachePolicy::NoCache. These win immediately: a malformed directive that follows them (no-store, max-age=abc) must not surface as a parse error.
Cache-Control: max-age=N (seconds) → CachePolicy::Ttl { ttl_ms: N * 1000 }. If stale-while-revalidate=M is also present → CachePolicy::StaleWhileRevalidate { ttl_ms: N * 1000, stale_ms: M * 1000 }.
Otherwise → CachePolicy::NoCache (no usable cache directives).

blocks.html: Four specifics:

items.html: s-maxage (the shared-cache directive) is a fallback: it applies only when max-age is absent, since this is a private cache.
Directive names are matched case-insensitively (Max-Age=60 works).
Values may be quoted (max-age="600").
Multiple Cache-Control headers combine; unknown directives (public, private) are ignored.

blocks.html: The three variants map exactly onto the policies described in Caching:

HttpCache<B> is a URL-keyed in-memory cache layered over an HttpBackend. Fresh entries short-circuit the network entirely; stale entries are revalidated with conditional headers and a 304 Not Modified re-serves the cached body without a new transfer.

HttpCache::fetch(&self, url: &str) -> Result<(Bytes, CachePolicy, Option<CacheMeta>), HttpError> returns the body, the policy in effect for this response, and the cached CacheMeta when the entry is cacheable.

HttpBackend is a trait that abstracts a single conditional GET. The crate ships one optional backend, ReqwestBackend, behind the reqwest cargo feature; reqwest is never a hard dependency. Any other request library can implement HttpBackend and plug into HttpCache::new:

The future is bound by MaybeSend (re-exported from gpui_query_http): exactly Send on native targets, a no-op bound on wasm32, so browser backends whose JS-interop futures are !Send still implement HttpBackend. Dispatch is static (HttpCache<B: HttpBackend>), so there is no Box<dyn> overhead, and the cache never requires tokio.
CacheMeta is the HTTP cache metadata extracted from a response. It holds the validators a backend resends to make a refetch cheap:

blocks.code:
pub struct CacheMeta {
    pub etag: Option<String>,
    pub last_modified: Option<String>,
    pub stored_at: std::time::SystemTime,
    pub fresh_for: Duration,
    pub stale_for: Duration,
}

blocks.html: With the persist feature on gpui-query, attach a serialized CacheMeta to a fetched value with Fetched::with_meta. It lands in PersistedEntry::meta and round-trips back through persistence, so after a relaunch the next fetch can send If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since and turn into a 304 with no body transfer:
This is what closes the loop with Persistence: the ETag survives a process restart, and hydration re-primes the cache.

items.html: Caching: how NoCache, Ttl, and StaleWhileRevalidate decide freshness.
Persistence: how meta travels through PersistedEntry and back via hydrate.

guides/query-keys.title: Query Keys
guides/query-keys.desc: Hierarchical, cheap-to-clone cache keys and the QueryKeyFilter for bulk operations

blocks.html: Every cached resource in gpui-query is identified by a QueryKey, a structured, hierarchical key inspired by TanStack Query’s array keys (["users", "42", "posts"]). Keys drive caching, deduplication, and the bulk operations (invalidate_queries, cancel_queries, reset_queries, remove_queries) that the QueryClient exposes.
A QueryKey is an ordered sequence of string segments. The simplest case is a single string:

blocks.code:
use gpui_query::QueryKey;

let key = QueryKey::from("users");

blocks.html: For resources scoped by an identifier, build a multi-segment key. The key records the order of the segments, so ["users", "42"] and ["42", "users"] are different keys.
You can construct a key from any of:

items.html: &str / String (single segment)
[&str; N], Vec<&str>, Vec<String> (multiple segments)
QueryKey::new(iterator) (panics on an empty iterator: a key must have at least one segment)

blocks.html: Internally a QueryKey stores its segments in an Arc<[Arc<str>]>, so cloning a key is a single atomic ref-count increment regardless of how many segments it holds. The hook layer and the QueryClient both clone keys freely (into buckets, into fetch tasks, into diagnostics).
Two methods make hierarchical keys useful:

items.html: starts_with(prefix): true when this key begins with prefix. This is the primitive the bulk operations use to invalidate a whole subtree.
to_path(): a users::42::posts-style display string for DevTools and logs. The :: separator avoids ambiguity when a segment itself contains a forward slash.

blocks.html: Adopt a convention where each segment narrows the scope: ["resource", "id", "view"]. Then ["users"] is the whole users subtree, ["users", "42"] is everything for user 42, and ["users", "42", "posts"] is that user’s posts. Bulk invalidation falls out of this naturally.

The options-first query hooks (use_query, use_query_with_policy, use_query_select, use_query_manual_opts, use_query_unsignalled_opts) take impl Into<QueryOptions>, so you can pass a bare string for the simple case or a structured key for a scoped resource. use_infinite_query is the exception: it takes InfiniteQueryOptions by value, so build one with InfiniteQueryOptions::new(QueryKey::from([...])) rather than passing a key directly. &str, String, QueryKey, QueryOptions, and (QueryKey, CachePolicy, RequestPolicy) tuples all convert; array and Vec keys convert only into QueryKey, so pass them as QueryKey::from(...) or build them through QueryOptions::new(...):
The bulk operations on QueryClient do not take a raw key; they take a QueryKeyFilter, which is how you say which keys to act on. There are three variants:

head: Filter
Matches
rows: Only the key that is exactly equal to k.
Every key that starts_with(k): the whole subtree.

blocks.html: QueryKeyFilter is Copy, so you can build it inline at the call site:

items.html: Exact when you know the full key (for example, after a mutation that updates a single record). invalidate_queries(Exact(&["users", "42"])) marks only that user stale; it refetches on its next access.

Prefix when a mutation affects a family of resources. For example, after creating a user, invalidate_queries(Prefix(&["users"])) marks the users list and every cached user stale; each refetches on its next access, since invalidation itself starts no request.
All for global resets, most commonly on logout: remove_queries(All) clears the cache, and reset_queries(All) clears data and cancels in-flight requests.

blocks.html: Keep the list and a detail view under a shared prefix so one invalidation refreshes both:

blocks.code:
let list = QueryKey::from(["users"]);
let detail = QueryKey::from(["users", id.as_str()]);

blocks.html: After an update mutation, invalidate_queries(Prefix(&["users"])) marks the list and any cached detail pages stale in one call; the next access to each refetches.
QueryKey only stores strings. To scope by a non-string id, format it into the key:

blocks.code: let key = QueryKey::from(["projects", &project_id.to_string(), "members"]);

blocks.html: QueryKey::new with a zero-length iterator panics. Every key must have at least one segment; there is no “root” key. Use QueryKeyFilter::All when you mean “everything”.

Caching: how CachePolicy interacts with keys.
Error handling: surfacing failures keyed by resource.

guides/select-pattern.title: The Select Pattern
guides/select-pattern.desc: Derive multiple views from one cached query with SelectTransform and use_query_select

blocks.html: TanStack Query’s select option transforms cached data into a derived shape. It re-runs only when the underlying data changes. gpui-query provides the same pattern through SelectTransform and the use_query_select hook. One cached query can feed several derived views without duplicating the cache entry.

blocks.text: Why select is a separate hook

blocks.html: In Rust the transform output type U has to be known at compile time. The QueryOptions struct is not generic over a transform output, so instead of making the whole options type generic, select lives on a dedicated hook: use_query_select. It accepts the transform as a separate parameter and returns a MappedQueryResource<T, U, E> entity.
The trade-off is ergonomic: select is a distinct hook rather than a field on options, but the type system stays simple.
A SelectTransform<T, U> wraps an Fn(&T) -> U closure. Build one with SelectTransform::new:
SelectTransform is Clone + Send + Sync (the closure is stored in an Arc), so you can share one transform across several mapped resources.

The hook wires a SelectTransform into the use_query lifecycle. It returns a triple: the mapped view entity, the underlying query entity, and the pair of subscriptions that keep both observations alive. Store both subscriptions. Dropping either breaks the observation.
Reading the derived value applies the transform lazily:

blocks.code:
// Inside a render / event handler that has cx:
let n: Option<usize> = count.read(cx).data();

blocks.html: use_query_select does three things:

items.html: Calls use_query to create and subscribe to the underlying QueryResource<T, E>.
Seeds a MappedQueryResource<T, U, E> with the query’s current data (one clone into an Arc<T>).

Observes the source entity and gates on its data epoch, a count of data writes rather than value changes. A notification that wrote no data (a retry tick, a pure status flip) does nothing at all; any data write re-stores via one T clone into a fresh Arc and notifies, including a refetch that returns identical content.

blocks.html: The upshot: notifications that wrote no data, the common case, cost nothing. A data write costs one T clone into a fresh Arc, identical content included. The transform itself is applied lazily, on every data() call.
Because the source data is shared, you can attach several mapped resources to the same underlying query, each with its own transform:
All three read from the same cached Vec<String>. Each MappedQueryResource stores only an Arc<T> to the shared source plus its own transform closure.

items.html: The transform closure runs every time MappedQueryResource::data() is called, and there is no output cache. For lightweight transforms (a field access, a .len()) the cost is negligible.

blocks.html: For expensive transforms called more than once in a render pass, cache the result in a local:

blocks.code:
let derived = mapped.read(cx).data(); // transform runs once
// reuse `derived` below instead of calling .data() again

items.html: The mapped entity notifies observers only when the source writes data, so derived views re-render at the cadence of data writes, not of status changes. Retry counts or status flips that leave data untouched cause no extra churn; a refetch that returns identical content still counts as a write.
Query keys: keys the underlying query is cached under.
Caching: how the source data’s CachePolicy controls refetch.
Observers: status deduplication for direct query subscriptions. The mapped resource above syncs through a raw observe plus a data-epoch check instead.

guides/claude-skills.title: Claude Code skills
guides/claude-skills.desc: Install gpui-query's Claude Code skills so your AI assistant writes correct hooks, caching, retry, and persistence code without guessing the API.

blocks.html: gpui-query ships two Claude Code skills: self-contained knowledge packs that teach an AI assistant the real gpui-query API (exact signatures, defaults, lifecycle, and gotchas). Install them once and the assistant stops guessing how use_query, CachePolicy, persist_with, or HttpCache work.

These use the standard Claude Code skill format, so they work in the Claude Code CLI, desktop app, web, and IDE extensions. They activate automatically based on what you’re working on. You don’t invoke them by hand.

head: Skill
Covers
rows: The essentials: use_query, use_mutation, use_infinite_query, use_query_select, in-memory CachePolicy (TTL / stale-while-revalidate / no-cache), RetryPolicy, QueryKey filters, QueryClient bulk operations, observers, and GC.

The satellite crates: HTTP Cache-Control → CachePolicy and an HttpCache layer for cheap 304 refetches (gpui-query-http), plus durable disk persistence with FilePersister and the persist feature (gpui-query-persist).

blocks.html: Install gpui-query for everyday app work; add gpui-query-extensions when you wire up HTTP caching or disk persistence.
Both skills live in the repo under skills/. Copy them into your user-level skills directory so they’re available in every project:

blocks.code: cp -R skills/gpui-query skills/gpui-query-extensions ~/.claude/skills/

blocks.html: Install a single skill, or fetch one without cloning the repo:

blocks.code:
# essentials
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/gpui-query
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/freeoxide/gpui-query/master/skills/gpui-query/SKILL.md \
  -o ~/.claude/skills/gpui-query/SKILL.md

# extensions
