blocks.html: After installing, open a project that depends on gpui-query and ask the assistant something about queries or caching. Run /skills to confirm both are registered.

To pin a skill to a single repo instead of every project, drop it into that project’s .claude/skills/ directory rather than ~/.claude/skills/. It then activates only when you’re working inside that project.

The skills track gpui-query v0.3.0 (essentials) and the v0.1.0 satellites (extensions). Each skill is a single SKILL.md with no other dependencies, so re-running the install command above after a cargo update refreshes them.

advanced/devtools.title: Devtools
advanced/devtools.desc: Inspect live query and mutation state in gpui-query: ClientDiagnostic snapshots and patterns for building a debug panel.

blocks.html: gpui-query exposes runtime diagnostics through the QueryClient. You get a point-in-time snapshot of every active query and mutation, which you can log or render in a debug panel.
Calling client.diagnostics(cx) returns a ClientDiagnostic struct. It is a point-in-time snapshot of the client internals.

items.html: query_count: number of query cache entries across all type buckets. An upper bound on queries.len(): entries whose entities were collected linger in the maps until the next GC sweep.
mutation_count: number of mutation cache entries, an upper bound on mutations.len() for the same reason.
queries: per-query diagnostics, one entry per resource.
mutations: per-mutation diagnostics (MutationDiagnostic: optional key, status, retry count), one entry per resource.

blocks.html: The struct derives Clone, Debug, and Default. You can render it in a GPUI debug panel or log it with Debug formatting.
Each entry in queries is a QueryDiagnostic:

blocks.code:
pub struct QueryDiagnostic {
    pub key: String,
    pub status: QueryStatus,
    pub cache_policy: String,
    pub cache_age_ms: Option<u64>,
    pub cache_hits: u64,
    pub retry_count: u32,
}

blocks.html: The fields:

head: Field
What it tells you
rows: The stringified QueryKey for this resource.
The QueryStatus enum value: Idle, LoadingEmpty, LoadingWithData, Success, Failure, or Cancelled. Call q.status.label() for the human-readable string.
Label from the configured CachePolicy: "No cache", "Cache TTL 60s", or "Stale-while-revalidate TTL 60s stale 60s".

Age in milliseconds of the last completed request, success or failure. None when no completed request is on record: never fetched, seeded via set_query_data, or invalidated. That does not mean the resource holds no data.
How many times this resource returned cached data instead of fetching.
How many retries the current or most recent fetch has attempted.

blocks.html: client.diagnostics(cx) returns a single snapshot covering every type bucket. There is no per-type accessor, so filter client-side over diag.queries (or diag.mutations) by key prefix:
Diagnostics are type-erased (key is a plain string), so a key prefix is the closest thing to per-type scoping when you are debugging a specific domain type.

blocks.text: Check whether your TTL is right

blocks.html: Use cache_age_ms to figure out how old cached data is. It is already an age in milliseconds, so there is no clock to read. If data is consistently stale, your CachePolicy::Ttl { ttl_ms } might be too long. If cache_hits is zero across the board, your TTL might be too short and every read triggers a refetch.

A high cache_hits count means the cache is doing its job. A count of zero on a resource that should be shared means you might be creating duplicate resources with slightly different keys. Check that your key construction is consistent.
Look at retry_count. A count at or near your RetryPolicy cap (3 retries by default) means the fetch keeps failing and the policy keeps re-attempting it, which points at a flaky or down endpoint.

blocks.text: Verify invalidation hit the right keys

blocks.html: After calling invalidate_queries on the QueryClient, run diagnostics again to see which keys the filter matched. Invalidation never changes status and never drops data, so a matched resource still reads Success. The signal is cache_age_ms: a matched key now reports None, because invalidation clears the last-updated timestamp that the age is computed from.

QueryDiagnostic derives only Clone and Debug, and ClientDiagnostic adds Default; neither implements Serialize. If you need JSON for a log aggregator, snapshot tests, or a debug panel that communicates over IPC, map the snapshot into your own serde types first: the snapshot itself exposes key and cache_policy as plain strings. The crate types behind it, QueryStatus and MutationStatus (the enums the diagnostics actually carry) plus the related CachePolicy, RequestPolicy, QueryKey, and QueryError, all implement Serialize/Deserialize.
If you are building a devtools panel in GPUI, consider polling diagnostics() on a timer. The cost is low: it reads entity state without cloning the actual cached data.

For real-time state tracking rather than point-in-time snapshots, see Observers. Observers subscribe to individual resource state changes, while diagnostics give you the full client picture in a single call. Use both together: diagnostics for the overview, observers for reactive updates on specific keys.

advanced/observers.title: Observers
advanced/observers.desc: Reactive subscriptions with status deduplication for queries, infinite queries, and mutations

blocks.html: Observers bridge gpui-query’s resources to GPUI’s reactivity. An observer attaches to a resource entity and calls cx.notify() to trigger a re-render, but only when the resource’s status or data changes. This is the primitive that keeps use_query, use_infinite_query, and use_mutation from re-rendering your view on every internal state mutation.
There is a single generic implementation, Observer<R>, parameterized over the resource kind. Three type aliases name the concrete observers you will use:
Each resource exposes its status via an inherent status() method; the public ObservableResource trait surfaces it generically so Observer<R> can deduplicate notifications for any resource kind.

Without status deduplication, a raw cx.observe would call cx.notify() on every entity mutation, including intermediate ones like increment_retry() that leave the status at Loading. A query retrying three times would re-render the view two or three extra times for nothing.
Observer tracks the last status and data epoch it saw and notifies only when either changes:

The result: increment_retry() / prepare_retry() calls (status stays Loading) no longer trigger re-renders. A same-status data write, such as set_query_data refreshing Success data, still re-renders: queries and infinite queries track a live data epoch, while MutationResource keeps the constant default and stays status-only. Your view re-renders on the transitions that matter: Idle → LoadingEmpty → Success, Success → LoadingWithData → Success, Loading → Failure, and so on.

Build an observer from an entity, then call observe(cx) to start watching. observe returns Option<Subscription> (None if the entity was already dropped). Store the returned subscription; dropping it ends the observation.

The hooks (use_query, use_infinite_query, use_mutation) already construct the observer and return the subscription for you. You only need to create an observer yourself when you are subscribing to a resource you obtained another way (for example, one you pulled out of the QueryClient with query::<T, E>(key)).
ObserverConfig::notify_on_status_change_only controls the dedup behavior. It defaults to true. Set it to false to get unconditional notifications on every entity mutation:
Use unconditional mode only when you need to react to non-status fields (a custom retry counter you display inline, for example). It is strictly more re-renders.

observe() returns Option<Subscription> rather than panicking. In debug builds the hooks panic! if this is None right after creating an entity (it would indicate a GPUI internal regression); in release builds they fall back to a no-op subscription so a misbehaving observer cannot crash the app. When you construct an observer yourself, decide explicitly: .expect(...) if a None is impossible in your context, or match / let else to handle it gracefully.

Each hook creates its observer, calls observe(cx), and returns the subscription as the second element of its tuple. The status-dedup is what makes a retrying mutation or a refetching query cheap to render: retry churn never reaches your view.

ObservableResource is the public trait that lets Observer<R> read a status generically. It is re-exported at gpui_query::client::ObservableResource and the crate root. It is why the three resource kinds share one observer implementation: each resource exposes status() with its own associated Status type, and Observer deduplicates on that. Implementing it requires observable_status(); data_epoch() defaults to 0, and a custom resource should override it when same-status data writes should still re-render. For application code, the three built-in observers cover every resource the hooks produce.

advanced/comparison.title: gpui-query vs. raw async
advanced/comparison.desc: What you stop writing when you move from cx.spawn and manual caching to gpui-query

blocks.html: GPUI already lets you run async work with cx.spawn and store the result on an entity. This page is a side-by-side: the same feature implemented with raw cx.spawn + manual state, then with gpui-query.
Fetching data in a GPUI view without a library means you end up reimplementing the same machinery every time:

items.html: A loading flag on the view.
A spawned task handle so a re-fetch or unmount cancels the old one.
A way to ignore the result of a stale request after the user typed again.
A cache somewhere so navigating back doesn’t refetch.
Retry on transient failures.
Re-rendering only when something the user can see actually changed.

blocks.html: Each one is small. Together they are the bulk of the code in a typical data-fetching view, and each is a place to introduce a subtle bug.

That is one resource, one view, no cache, no retry, and it already has a latent stale-write bug. Add a second view that needs the same user and you are either refetching or hand-rolling a shared cache.
What you got for free:

head: Concern
Raw cx.spawn
gpui-query
rows: QueryObserver skips same-status bookkeeping, wakes on status or data change

blocks.text: When the raw approach is enough

blocks.html: gpui-query is not free. It is a dependency and a mental model. The raw approach is fine when:

items.html: You have one async operation that does not need to be cached or shared.
The result is not something a second view will ever want.
There is no retry, no dedup, and no stale-write concern (a fire-and-forget side effect, for example).

blocks.html: For those cases cx.spawn plus a field on the view is the right tool. gpui-query earns its keep the moment a second view needs the same data, the user can trigger a re-fetch while one is in flight, or you want the app to feel instant because data is already cached.

With QueryClient set as a global, every use_query call with the same key resolves to the same resource entity. Two views that both need ["users", "42"] get one fetch, one cache entry, and consistent state. A third view mounted later reads straight from the cache.

blocks.code:
// Set once, in app setup:
cx.set_global(gpui_query::QueryClient::new());

blocks.html: That cache is also what makes bulk operations possible: invalidate_queries(Prefix(&["users"])) refreshes the whole users subtree in one call, and remove_queries(All) clears the cache on logout. With raw cx.spawn you have no central registry, so there is nothing to invalidate or clear.
gpui-query still gives you the imperative escape hatches you would write by hand:

items.html: fetch_query: refetch on demand (button click, timer).
QueryClient::prepare_fetch_query / prepare_prefetch_query: fetch or prefetch without subscribing, the equivalent of queryClient.fetchQuery / prefetchQuery.
get_query_data / set_query_data: read or seed the cache directly for optimistic updates.

blocks.html: The difference is that these operate on the shared, deduplicated, GC’d cache rather than on ad-hoc fields scattered across your views.

Reach for raw cx.spawn for one-off fire-and-forget work. Reach for gpui-query the moment you are caching, sharing, retrying, or guarding against stale writes. For anything that talks to a server, that is usually the first feature you need.

advanced/migration.title: Migrating from v1 to v2
advanced/migration.desc: The breaking and behavioral changes from gpui-query v1 to the options-first v2 API

blocks.html: gpui-query v2 (the main crate since 0.1.1, when the rewrite replaced the v1 API now frozen in gpui-query-legacy) is an options-first redesign. The hooks keep the same names, but the call signatures, return types, and a number of internal behaviors changed. This page is a checklist for porting a v1 codebase to v2, grouped by what breaks. The current release is 0.3.0, and its changelog entry lists only fixes and additive changes, so every step here applies to 0.3.x unchanged.

The biggest mechanical change is the call signature. v1 took the key, cache policy, and request policy as separate positional arguments. v2 takes a single QueryOptions (or a bare key string, which converts via Into).
For the simplest case (a key with default policies), pass the string directly:

blocks.code: let (entity, _sub) = use_query("users", |signal| async move { Ok(vec![]) }, cx);

blocks.html: v2 hooks return (Entity<…>, Subscription). You must store the Subscription or the observation is dropped immediately and your view will not re-render on data changes.

The change is use_mutation, which returned a bare Entity in v1. use_query already returned (Entity, Subscription), and use_infinite_query returned a triple ending in the Subscription; v2 returns the pair and moves the refetch closure out to fetch_next_page_infinite. use_query_select returns a triple including a second subscription for the mapped observer; store both.

v2 fetchers always receive a QuerySignal. If you have long-running fetches, check signal.is_cancelled() periodically to bail out early when a newer request supersedes yours. For short fetches you can ignore it: the two-phase accept_current_request guard discards stale results automatically.
If you cannot change the fetcher signature, use_query_unsignalled keeps the Fn() -> Fut (no-signal) shape for backward compatibility. It is not the recommended default.

blocks.text: 4. Mutation retry defaults did not change

blocks.html: Mutations default to RetryPolicy::no_retries() in both v1 and v2, because silently retrying a destructive action is dangerous. What changed in v2 is the call shape: use_mutation now takes options first, and use_mutation((), cx) keeps the same no-retries, 5-minute GC defaults (see section 5). If your mutation is idempotent and you want retries, opt in explicitly:
The old options-taking mutation hook, deprecated in 0.2.0, has been removed. use_mutation accepts MutationOptions via Into, so one hook covers both shapes:
If you were still on the deprecated hook, switch to the opts form above; the call reads the same and nothing else changes.
v1 infinite queries accumulated pages without limit. v2 defaults to max_pages: Some(50) to prevent unbounded memory growth from deep scrolling. If you need unbounded pages, opt back in:

blocks.code:
use gpui_query::hook::InfiniteQueryOptions;

let opts = InfiniteQueryOptions::new("feed").unbounded_pages();

blocks.html: Otherwise, decide on a cap that fits your UI (max_pages(n)).
v2 gives QueryError full Display + Error impls, so it composes with ? and anyhow. You can now return it from fallible helpers directly:
And use QueryError::sanitized() at the boundary where you convert server responses, so tokens and connection strings do not leak into logs or DevTools.

v1 re-rendered views on every internal mutation (including retry ticks). v2’s QueryObserver / MutationObserver deduplicates by status, so a retrying query no longer re-renders your view on every attempt; since 0.3.0 the query observers also re-render on data-only writes to an already-Success entry (set_query_data, hydrate, prefetch completion), so optimistic updates reach the view while retry ticks stay silent. MutationObserver still dedupes by status alone. You can remove manual “did the status actually change?” guards from your render logic.

items.html: QueryKey and the hierarchical key model are unchanged.

QueryKeyFilter (Exact / Prefix / All) is unchanged, but remove_queries dropped its cx argument: call it as client.remove_queries(&filter). invalidate_queries and reset_queries keep their v1 (filter, cx) signatures, and cancel_queries is new in v2.

RequestPolicy and its semantics are unchanged. CachePolicy is not: StaleWhileRevalidate gained a stale_ms field (v1 had only ttl_ms), so v1 constructions of that variant must add it, and v2 serves fresh data within ttl_ms, then stale data with a background revalidation until ttl_ms + stale_ms. v1 SWR never short-circuited; every fetch ran.

The QueryClient is still a GPUI Global, but the constructor changed: v1’s QueryClient::new(cache_policy, request_policy) becomes QueryClient::new() in v2, so the setup line reads cx.set_global(QueryClient::new()). Pass custom defaults via QueryClient::with_policies(cache_policy, request_policy).
Cancellation is still cooperative via QuerySignal; only the staleness guard is stricter (no more TOCTOU window).
